---
title: "Session 4: Prepare to Publish!"
---

## Overview

The hard work is done — you have a reproducible environment, version-controlled code, and a collaborative workflow. Now let's make it citable.

---

## The final hurdles

Before sharing code publicly alongside a manuscript, four things are typically missing:

- ❌ **No licence** — legally, no one can reuse your code
- ❌ **No release** — no stable, citable snapshot
- ❌ **No DOI** — no way to cite it in a paper
- ❌ **No data repository** — raw data has nowhere to live

---

## Licensing

::: {.callout-important}
Code without a licence is **not** open source — it is legally unusable. Without a licence, nobody has permission to reuse, modify, or distribute your work, even if it is publicly visible on GitHub.
:::

A licence is just a text file — `LICENSE` — in the root of your repository. It tells anyone who finds your code exactly what they are and are not allowed to do with it.

### Common licences for code

| Licence | Use freely | Modify & distribute | Must stay open | Commercial use |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **MIT** | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| **Apache 2.0** | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| **GPL v3** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

::: {.callout-note}
**MIT** is the most common choice for research code — permissive, simple, and well understood. **GPL** is appropriate if you want derivative work to remain open.
:::

### Licences for data & documents

- **CC BY 4.0** — free to use and share with attribution. Most common for research data.
- **CC0** — no rights reserved. Maximum reuse, no attribution required. Used by many data repositories.
- **CC BY-NC** — non-commercial use only. Restrictive — consider carefully whether this is what you want.

::: {.callout-tip}
A common pairing: **MIT** for your code + **CC BY 4.0** for your data.
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
### Exercises

4.1 Browse [choosealicense.com](https://choosealicense.com)

4.2 Decide on a licence for your `spacewalk_analysis` repository

4.3 Add a `LICENSE` file with the relevant text and commit
:::

## Releases

A GitHub **release** is a named snapshot of your repository at a point in time — typically tied to a paper submission or publication.

Releases use **semantic versioning**: `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`

- `v1.0.0` — first stable, publication-ready version
- `v1.1.0` — new features added after publication
- `v1.0.1` — bug fix, no new features

::: {.callout-tip}
For most research code, `v1.0.0` is the only release you will ever make — and that is completely fine.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
A GitHub release is a stable snapshot — but it is **not permanent**. It can be deleted or renamed, has no DOI, and cannot be cited in a paper on its own.
:::

---

## Zenodo: Making your code citable

[**Zenodo**](https://zenodo.org) is an open research repository hosted by CERN. It will:

- Archive a permanent copy of your code
- Issue a **DOI** that can be cited in papers
- Index your work so others can find it

GitHub and Zenodo work together: when you create a release on GitHub, Zenodo automatically mints a DOI for that release, plus a persistent DOI for the entire repository.

### Workflow

::: {.callout-tip}
Today we will use [sandbox.zenodo.org](https://sandbox.zenodo.org) — a practice environment that issues test DOIs. It requires a separate account from zenodo.org, but the experience is identical.
:::

1. Go to [sandbox.zenodo.org](https://sandbox.zenodo.org) and sign in
2. Navigate to your account → **GitHub**
3. Find your repository in the list and **toggle it on**
4. Go to your repository on GitHub and create a new **Release** (tag: `v1.0.0`)
5. Return to Zenodo — your DOI will appear within a few minutes

::: {.callout-caution}
### Exercises

4.4 Make the repository public (`Settings → General → Change repository visibility`)

4.5 Link your GitHub account to [sandbox.zenodo.org](https://sandbox.zenodo.org) and enable tracking of your repository

4.6 Create a `v1.0.0` release — then watch Zenodo mint your DOI
:::

## README extras

### DOI badge

Zenodo provides a DOI badge for your release — copy the Markdown snippet and paste it into your `README.md`.

Other badges (licence, latest release, build status) can be generated at [shields.io](https://shields.io).

```markdown
[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.xxxxxx.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.xxxxxx)
```

### `CITATION.cff`

A `CITATION.cff` file tells GitHub — and anyone who finds your repo — exactly how to cite your work. GitHub renders it as a **"Cite this repository"** button automatically.

```yaml
cff-version: 1.2.0
message: "If you use this software, please cite it as below."
authors:
  - family-names: Cox
    given-names: Dezerae
    orcid: https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000
title: "Spacewalk Analysis"
version: 1.0.0
doi: 10.5072/zenodo.xxxxxx
date-released: 2026-04-22
```

::: {.callout-tip}
[cffinit](https://citation-file-format.github.io/cff-initializer-javascript/) generates a valid `CITATION.cff` in your browser — no syntax knowledge needed.
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
### Exercises

4.7 Copy the DOI badge from your Zenodo record and add it to `README.md`

4.8 Use [cffinit](https://citation-file-format.github.io/cff-initializer-javascript/) to generate a `CITATION.cff`, add it to your repository, and push — check the **"Cite this repository"** button appears on GitHub
:::

## Data repositories

GitHub is the right home for your **code** — but it is not built for **data**.

- ❌ GitHub has a 100 MB file size limit
- ❌ Large files bloat your repository history
- ❌ Raw data should not be version-controlled alongside code
- ❌ GitHub repos can be deleted — DOIs from data repositories cannot

::: {.callout-note}
Raw data belongs in a **data repository** — a permanent, citable, indexed home designed for research outputs.
:::

### Discipline-specific repositories

| Repository | Best for | Discipline |
|---|---|---|
| [PRIDE](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pride/) | Proteomics (mass spec) | Proteomics |
| [GEO](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/) | Gene expression data | Genomics |
| [SRA](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra/) | Raw sequencing data | Genomics |
| [BioImage Archive](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/bioimage-archive/) | Biological imaging | Imaging |
| [OpenNeuro](https://openneuro.org) | Neuroimaging (MRI, EEG) | Neuroimaging |
| [PANGAEA](https://www.pangaea.de) | Environmental & Earth science | Spatial |
| [GBIF](https://www.gbif.org) | Biodiversity & occurrence data | Ecology |

::: {.callout-tip}
Can't find a match? [re3data.org](https://www.re3data.org) indexes 2,000+ repositories — search by subject, data type, or country.
:::

### General repositories

| Repository | Best for |
|---|---|
| [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org) | Any research output |
| [Figshare](https://figshare.com) | Figures, datasets, code |
| [OSF](https://osf.io) | Full projects + preprints |

::: {.callout-tip}
When in doubt, **Zenodo** or **Figshare** accept almost anything — but many journals mandate a discipline-specific repository. Always check first.
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
### Exercises

4.9 For each data type you work with, identify the standard or recommended repository — start with your target journal's data availability policy

4.10 Are there any data types without a discipline-specific home? Note them — **Zenodo** or **Figshare** are your fallback
:::

## Pre-publication checklist

Before making your repository public:

- ✅ **Structure** — does it follow the standard layout?
- ✅ **Clean code** — hardcoded paths, dead code, debug prints, TODOs, irregular naming all removed
- ✅ **No raw data or results** in the repo (in `.gitignore` and preferably in a data repository)
- ✅ **README** — could a stranger clone and run your code from this alone?
- ✅ **Environment file** — is `environment.yml` or `renv.lock` up to date?
- ✅ **Licence** — is a `LICENSE` file present with an appropriate licence?
- ✅ **No credentials** — API keys, passwords, tokens all removed

::: {.callout-tip}
You do not need perfection — simply clarity. A stranger (or future you) should be able to clone, run, and understand your code independently.
:::

## Where to from here?

**Tools & platforms**

- [re3data.org](https://www.re3data.org) — registry of research data repositories
- [Quarto Manuscripts](https://quarto.org/docs/manuscripts/) — publish code and data integrated into manuscripts
- [Code Ocean](https://codeocean.com) — platform for executable code capsules
- [Snakemake](https://snakemake.readthedocs.io/en/stable/) — automate reproducible workflows
- [GitHub templates](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/creating-a-repository-from-a-template) — standardised repo structures

**Reading & learning**

- [FAIR principles](https://www.go-fair.org/fair-principles/) — Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable
- [The Turing Way](https://book.the-turing-way.org/) — comprehensive handbook for reproducible research
- [Software Carpentry: Better Research Software](https://carpentries-incubator.github.io/better-research-software/)
- [ReproducibiliTea](https://www.reproducibilitea.org/) — journal club and community for reproducible research
